The left half of @fig-sam-size picks the story up in 2016, after that big drop, and its most recent chapter
is a partial rebound. In 2016 base defense was on the field for 31% of
snaps; by 2023 it was down to 22%. Then it came back:
31% in 2025, close to the 29.7% Next Gen Stats measured, because offenses
returned to two-tight-end and fullback sets and defenses answered with bigger personnel.[^ngsbase] The Sam
didn't disappear; he became a part-time player.

The other half of the story is the linebackers who stayed. If two linebackers are going to be on the field for
most snaps, and those two have to cover running backs and tight ends in space as well as fill gaps, teams want
them faster, and faster usually means lighter. The right half of @fig-sam-size shows the trend at the NFL
Combine. Off-ball linebackers in the 2000–2009 draft classes averaged 242
pounds and ran the 40-yard dash in 4\.75 seconds; the classes since 2019
have averaged 233 pounds and 4\.60
seconds.[^combine] Nine or ten pounds and a tenth and a half of a second doesn't sound like much. At the second level it
is the difference between running with a running back and watching him.

The clearest sign of the shift is where some linebackers come from. In 2015 the Arizona Cardinals moved Deone
Bucannon, a safety they had drafted in the first round a year earlier, to inside linebacker, at about 211
pounds. Their depth chart listed him as "$ILB," and the coaches called him the *moneybacker*: a safety's speed
and coverage in a linebacker's spot, playing the run by beating blockers to the hole rather than taking them
on.[^bucannon] Other teams followed with safety-sized linebackers and linebacker-sized safeties, until in some
defenses the line between the two positions is mostly a matter of which word is on the depth chart. The big
nickel of [A First Look at Defense](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd), with a
third safety in the box, is the same idea from the other direction.

What the safety-sized linebacker gives up is the thing the Sam was built for: taking on a fullback or a pulling
guard in the hole and holding his ground. A 215-pound linebacker who has to stand still and absorb a 315-pound
guard loses. So the modern linebacker is coached to *not* stand still: to beat the blocker to the spot, or run
through the gap before he arrives, the fits from earlier in this chapter. The best of today's linebackers
combine both. San Francisco's Fred Warner, a third-round pick in 2018 and first-team All-Pro in 2020, 2022, 2023
and 2024, is about 6-foot-3 and 230 pounds: the coverage linebacker teams hoped the safety-sized linebacker would
be, in a full-sized body. Watch him carry a tight end up the seam in his zone drops, the hook/curl seam carry of
@fig-hook-curl, and then fill against the run.[^warner] And when offenses go heavy,
with two tight ends and a fullback, as many did again in 2025, defenses bring back a third linebacker, or a
bigger one. The Sam isn't extinct. He is a specialist who comes in when the offense does.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"Linebackers are the defense's run-stoppers; the defensive backs cover." In the modern NFL the two off-ball
linebackers are on the field for most passing snaps and are in coverage on most of them, against running backs,
tight ends and slot receivers. A linebacker who cannot cover cannot stay on the field, however well he tackles.
That, more than anything, is what has changed about the position.
:::

## The green dot: the defense's quarterback

One linebacker usually has one more job, and it starts before anyone moves. Since 2008 NFL rules have allowed
one defensive player on the field to have a radio speaker in his helmet, the way quarterbacks have since 1994;
the owners approved it by a single vote over the required majority.[^radio] That player wears the
[green dot](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-green-dot) sticker you met in
[What a Play Really Is](../01-foundations/01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd), and the radio cuts off with 15
seconds on the play clock. On most teams, he is the Mike.

Against a trips formation with the tight end attached on the right, the Mike (green ring) hears the call in his helmet and relays it, then sets the defense to the formation he sees: the strength, the front, the coverage, then any adjustment to a motion or shift, and the alerts from the week's film study.](05-04-linebackers-and-second-level_files/figure-html/fig-green-dot-output-1.svg){#fig-green-dot}
:::
:::


What does he actually do with it?

1. **He relays the call.** The defensive coordinator calls the front, the coverage and any pressure into one
   helmet. The green dot passes it to the other ten, in a huddle or with hand signals, before the radio goes
   dead.
2. **He sets the strength.** Every rule in the call depends on which side is "strong," and the strength
   depends on what the offense shows: the tight end, the trips side, the running back, or the wide side of
   the field. The green dot decides and shouts it, and the front sets off his word, the way
   [Even Fronts](05-02-even-fronts.qmd) showed. The hard part is that many defenses set the *front* to the
   tight end (or the back) and the *coverage* to the receivers. In @fig-green-dot they agree; against trips
   with the tight end on the other side they don't, and he has to call both: "Front left, coverage right."
3. **He adjusts to what the offense does.** When the offense shifts or sends a man in motion, the strength may
   change, and with it the front and the coverage rules. With the radio already off, the green dot is the one
   who re-sets everyone, in a second or two, with a word. (If the offense substitutes after the radio has
   cut out, a new call comes from the sideline by hand signal, and he passes it on.)
4. **He makes the alerts.** Linebackers study opponents' tendencies all week. The green dot is the one who
   sees a formation and yells "Watch the screen!" or "Boot! Boot!" before the snap, from a list built in film
   study.
5. **He plays a game with the protection.** The offense's center identifies a defender as the "Mike" for its
   blocking count, the [Mike identification](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-mike-identification) of
   [Pass Protection](../04-the-passing-game/04-02-pass-protection.qmd). The defense knows it. Linebackers walk
   up, back out and swap spots before the snap to make that identification wrong.

It is a lot to ask of one player, and it is why teams prize linebackers who are, in the clichéd but accurate
phrase, coaches on the field. It is also why the green dot has started to move. A linebacker who comes off the
field in some packages takes the radio with him, and the backup green dot has to take over. More and more teams
have given the radio to a safety or another defensive back who never leaves the field: six teams did in 2021,
according to one count.[^greendotdb] The Mike's job doesn't vanish when he loses the dot; he still sets the
front and the run fits in the box, while the safety with the radio runs the coverage.

## Film room

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Baltimore Ravens 2000"}
**The season:** Ray Lewis's Ravens allowed 165 points in 16 games, the fewest
in a 16-game season, and 970 rushing yards, also a 16-game record, then beat
the Giants 34–7 in Super Bowl XXXV; Lewis was the game's MVP and the league's Defensive Player of the
Year.[^ravens2000]

**Where to look:** Super Bowl XXXV, against the Giants. **What to notice:** the two big defensive tackles in
front of him, Tony Siragusa and Sam Adams. Their job was to occupy both guards so that nobody could climb to
Lewis: watch the guards at the snap, then watch how often Lewis gets to the ball without anyone touching him.
This is the *protected* linebacker at his best (the opposite of the open linebacker over a free guard): two
big tackles who keep the guards off him, and a linebacker fast enough to his keys to make that pay.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Carolina Panthers 2015"}
**The season:** the Panthers went 15–1 and reached Super Bowl 50 with Luke Kuechly at middle linebacker, three
seasons after he was the Defensive Rookie of the Year and two after he became the youngest Defensive Player of
the Year. In the playoffs that January he returned interceptions for touchdowns in both of Carolina's NFC
games, the first in the opening minutes against Seattle and the second in the 49–15 NFC Championship win over
Arizona.[^kuechly]

**Where to look:** the NFC Championship Game against Arizona. **What to notice:** Kuechly's first step. He was
famous for moving before the play had declared itself, and on the replay you can usually see why: his eyes are
on a guard or the back, and he goes where they tell him. On passing downs, watch him in the hole, reading the
quarterback and driving on throws in front of him. He retired in January 2020,
at 28.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Baltimore Ravens 2022"}
**The trade:** On October 31, 2022, Chicago traded Roquan Smith, the eighth pick of the 2018 draft, to Baltimore
for a second-round pick, a fifth-round pick and a linebacker; in January 2023 the Ravens signed him to a
five-year, $100 million extension, the first for an off-ball linebacker at $20 million a year.[^roquan] In the
eight games before he arrived, the Ravens allowed 22\.9 points a game; in the nine
after, 14\.7. (Not all of that was Smith: other starters returned from injuries,
and the schedule changed. But the timing was hard to miss.)[^ravens22]

**Where to look:** his first game for Baltimore, a 27–13 win at New Orleans on Monday night, November 7.
**What to notice:** a modern run-through linebacker. Watch Smith's fills against zone runs: he is through the
gap before the climbing lineman gets there, which is how a 235-pound linebacker beats a guard who outweighs him
by 80 pounds. Then watch him and Patrick Queen, the other inside linebacker that season, talk before the snap,
and how often they swap responsibilities after the offense shifts.
:::

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it"}
**Mirror the Mike.** For ten snaps, watch only the middle linebacker. Ignore the ball.

- **Before the snap:** Where is he standing: stacked behind a lineman, open over a guard, or walked out over a
  receiver? Is he pointing and shouting? (That's the green dot setting the strength.) Does anyone walk up into
  the A gaps?
- **At the snap: first steps forward or back?** His very first step is a short read step; the *second* one
  tells you what he saw. Forward, it's a run, or he thinks it is. Back, it's a pass. Sideways means he has read
  a pull or zone flow; see which way he goes and where the ball goes.
- **On runs:** Did he fill, plug, scrape or run through? Did a guard get to him? Was he inside the ball as
  he pursued, or did the back cut back behind him?
- **On passes:** Did he drop to a spot, run with a back or a tight end, or rush? On play-action, count his
  steps forward before he turned around.
- **On the replay:** Watch the guards and the back, his keys. Did they tell the truth?

For your prediction log ([How to Watch a Broadcast](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd)):
write *F* or *B* for the Mike's first real step, then *run* or *pass*. After a half, check how often his first step
was right, and which plays fooled him.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 1. The back says one thing, the linemen another.** First-and-10, shotgun, the back to the quarterback's
right. In the first quarter-second after the snap the back takes a step to his *right*, while the right guard
and right tackle pull to the *left*. You are the Mike. Which way do you go, and what is the play?

::: {#cell-fig-drill-1 .cell execution_count=17}
``` {.python .cell-code}
off = line("full") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, 2.2, "R")]
p = Play(off, nickel_front(mike=(4.7, 0.2), will=(4.7, -2.2)), los=35, to_go=10,
         title="Drill 1: the back steps right, two linemen pull left")
go_to(p, "RB", (-4.5, 3.6), "run")
go_to(p, "RG", (-1.5, -0.8), via=[(-1.5, 1.0)])
go_to(p, "RT", (-1.9, 1.0), via=[(-1.8, 2.8)])
for k in ("LT", "LG", "C"):
    q = p.players[k]
    go_to(p, k, (q.d + 0.4, q.w + 0.9), "block")
go_to(p, "Y", (-1.6, 5.0), "block")              # hinge: step back and wall off the backside end
p.highlight("MIKE", color=style.DEFENSE)
p.read("RB", key="MIKE"); p.read("RG", key="MIKE")
f = draw(p, width_in=5.4, lateral=(-9.0, 9.6), window=(-7.6, 7.6))
plt.show()
```

![Drill 1: the first quarter-second. The back steps right (short arrow); the right guard and right tackle step flat to the left behind the line (their pulls); the left side of the line blocks down to the right, and the tight end steps back. The Mike (ringed) is reading the back and the right guard (dotted).](05-04-linebackers-and-second-level_files/figure-html/fig-drill-1-output-1.svg){#fig-drill-1}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Go left, with the guard and tackle. It's counter.** The back's step to the right is the counter step, the lie
the play is built on ([Gap and Power Runs](../03-the-run-game/03-03-gap-and-power-runs.qmd)); the two pullers are
the truth, because two linemen can't run to the left unless the ball is going there. The guard will kick out the
end man on the left, and the tackle will wrap through the hole looking for the play-side linebacker, the Will.
(On the right, the tight end steps back to wall off the end the pulling tackle left: a *hinge*.)

You are the backside linebacker. Your guard has just pulled, so you follow him: sideways toward the offense's
left (your right), flat and inside-out, while the center or left guard tries to climb to you, and you fill the
hole the tackle leads through. It is the read in @fig-key-pull, from the other side. A Mike who believes the back
takes a false step toward him, and by the time he recovers the hole has opened behind his back. This is the
textbook case for "if your keys disagree, believe the linemen."
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 2. The walk-out that gives it away.** Third-and-6. The offense is in 11 personnel with the back beside
the quarterback. Before the snap the back motions out of the backfield and lines up wide on the left. The Will
linebacker walks out with him and stands over him. What did the defense just tell you, and what is the offense
likely to do?

::: {#cell-fig-drill-2 .cell execution_count=18}

off = line("short") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -1.6, "R"),
                       O("X", "WR", -0.7, -17.0, "X"), O("H", "WR", -1.5, -8.6, "H"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 15.0, "Z")]

    D("NB", "NB", 3.0, -8.6, "$"), D("SS", "S", 7.6, 6.0, "SS"), D("FS", "S", 13.5, 0.0, "FS"),
    D("LCB", "CB", 3.0, -17.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 3.0, 15.0, "CB")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=6, title="Drill 2: the back goes out, the Will goes with him")
p.motion("RB", to=(-1.5, -12.8))
p.highlight("WILL", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, width_in=6.0, lateral=(-20.4, 18.4), window=(-7.6, 16.4))
dashed(f, p, [(4.6, -2.9), (4.4, -8.0), (4.0, -12.0)], color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=1.3)
ghost(f, p, 4.0, -12.8, "W")

![Drill 2: the back (R) motions out to the left, between the slot receiver (H) and the split end (X); the Will (ringed) walks out of the box and follows him (dashed). One deep safety; the cornerbacks and the nickel back are tight on their receivers.](05-04-linebackers-and-second-level_files/figure-html/fig-drill-2-output-1.svg){#fig-drill-2}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The defense told you it is in man coverage, and it told you which matchup the offense now has: a running back
against a linebacker, in space, on third down.** A zone defense would have let the back go and simply re-set its
zones; a defense that sends a specific defender with a man who moves is matching him (the motion-as-indicator
idea from [Motion and Shifts](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-06-motion-and-shifts.qmd)). With one deep safety,
the coverage is probably Cover 1.

The offense will usually go to that matchup: a quick route for the back, a slant, a quick out or an option route,
where his quickness against a linebacker who has never covered him from out there is worth six yards. It is the
case for linebackers who can cover, and for the safety-sized linebackers who replaced the Sam. Two smaller
points: the box has lost a defender, leaving five (four linemen and the Mike) against six blockers, so a quarterback draw is suddenly
attractive; and a well-coached defense may answer the motion by swapping assignments ("banjo," or switching the
nickel back onto the back) so that the linebacker never ends up out there at all. A [banjo](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-banjo)
is the general version: two defenders trade who covers whom depending on where the receivers go.
:::
:::

the back sprints for the tight end's outside leg. The picture is frozen 0.8 seconds after the snap; compare it
with the fast-flow half of @fig-flow. Both
linebackers have flowed hard to the right. Where does the back go, and who made the mistake?

lane(fld, p, -3.6, 0.4, 1.9, 6.4, color=style.OFFENSE, alpha=0.10)

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The back cuts back, behind the Will, into the backside A or B gap, and the Will made the mistake.** Outside
zone is built to make the defense run sideways and then to cut against the flow
([Zone Running](../03-the-run-game/03-02-zone-running.qmd)). The play-side linebacker, the Mike, is right to run
with it, inside-out. But the Will is the backside linebacker, and his job against fast flow is to follow a step
behind the Mike and a little deeper, *over the top*, as the cutback player (@fig-flow). Here he is level with the
Mike and nearly as far over as the ball, so the shaded area behind the line's flow is empty except for linemen
who are being cut off. The back plants his foot and goes there, and the next defender is a safety.

A good Will gives up a yard or two to the outside to keep the cutback: if the back keeps going, the Mike and the
Sam are there, and the Will arrives late but in the right place. He doesn't hold the cutback alone; the backside
end has to squeeze or chase so the back can't bend it all the way back. The cutback runs you see go for 20 yards
are usually a backside player out of place: a linebacker who ran too fast, an end who got reached or cut, or a
safety who flowed too early.
:::
:::

## Back to the huddle

The chapter opened with a middle linebacker who went the "wrong" way, away from the back's jab step, and
stopped the run for no gain, while the analyst circled the left guard. Now you can see what he saw. The guard
nearest him fired out (a run), and the left guard opened his hips and ran flat behind the line (a pull, so a
gap-scheme run going where he went). The back's jab step was window dressing. The Mike went with the puller, had
the shorter trip, and met him at the line, where the hole was supposed to be. The back never had a chance to
choose.

## Takeaways

- **Where a linebacker stands is a trade.** Stacked behind a lineman, he is shielded and hard to read but a step
  slower to the gaps; open over an uncovered guard, he sees everything and is easy to block; walked out to an apex over a slot receiver, he can
  cover but he has left the box light and become the offense's conflict defender.
- **Linebackers read keys, not the ball.** The guards' first steps (fire out, down block, pull, zone step, pass
  set) and the near back's direction tell him run or pass and where, early enough to get there. The offense knows it, which is
  why counters, traps and play-action are built to make his keys lie.
- **Flow tells him how to move; the fit tells him where.** Fast flow: run with it, inside-out, with the backside
  linebacker a step behind for the cutback. Slow flow: press the gap and stay square. The fit is a fill, a plug, a
  scrape or a run-through, and the scrape is also the defense's answer to the zone read.
- **The second level is where runs are decided.** Pursuit angles aim where the runner will be, a step inside him,
  with a leverage player outside; leverage tackling takes away one direction and wraps the legs. Inside linebackers
  make a fifth to a quarter of the tackles on runs up to 9 yards; misses rise with the space around the tackle,
  and a run that beats the linebackers is a defensive back's tackle.
- **On passes, linebackers are hook/curl defenders, man defenders on backs and tight ends, robbers in the hole and
  blitzers.** Play-action targets their keys; the uncovered guard who doesn't climb is the tell.
- **The position has shrunk.** Spread offenses made the Sam a part-time player, replaced by a nickel back, and made
  the remaining linebackers lighter and faster, down to safety-sized "moneybackers." The green-dot linebacker, who sets the
  strength and adjusts the defense before every snap, is the job that hasn't changed.
